Q: How can I merge multiple lines into one line in Vim? A:

In Command-line mode:

:[range]j[lines]

For example: here you want to do the whole buffer:

:%j

If you just wanted to do 10 lines from the current cursor position:

:j10

If you don’t want to replace the new lines with spaces, use ! after j.

:%j!
:j!10

And for the uberfancy:

:5j20

This would go to line 5, and join the next 20 lines.

Q: I'm looking for docs on how to package my app in a docker container and make it accessible via a browser A:

Docker is probably not the tool you're looking for here. You need something that runs a virtual X server and makes its display accessible over an HTTP connection. That almost certainly exists, but it's not Docker per se.

If you have a Gtk+ app it will not run well in Docker, and Docker will not magically make it browser-accessible. A Docker container provides an isolated environment with its own filesystem and networking layer, and it doesn't really do much beyond run a single program in that isolated environment. This means it can't see the host's X server socket (see Can you run GUI applications in a Linux Docker container? for the machinations involved) or any of the settings in the user's home directory.

A Docker container runs a single process. It is not a VM. It does not run a display server. It does not fundamentally transform the process it's running, so if it's already running a Web server it can make it easier to reproducibly deploy it, but if it's not, then Docker won't add one.

At a very mechanical level, your program is expecting to make an outbound connection to a Unix socket in /tmp/.X0-unix, and you want it to accept inbound connections on port 443. That's a very different action.

A typical application setup these days is to break an application into a back-end component and a front-end component. The back-end serves an HTTP API and has no display logic at all, and can be written in any language with an HTTP server (IME this largely means something newer than C/C++). The front-end must be written in Javascript (or compiled to Javascript) and runs in the end user's browser. The two components could run in two separate containers, or you could compile the front-end to static Javascript files and serve them from the back-end container. Docker is a better fit for this type of setup (though note you do not need to force Docker into your core development process, only use it for integration testing and deployment) but it would involve a major rewrite of your application.

If you want to investigate further, Docker has a set of official documentation; maybe Writing a Dockerfile is as good a starting point as any these days.

Q: What data distribution strategies does GBase 8a support besides hash? A:

In GBase 8a, data distribution determines how rows are physically distributed across nodes in the cluster. Besides hash distribution, the following strategies are supported:

  • Replication
    Description: A full copy of the table is stored on every node.
    Recommended scenarios: Small dimension tables that are frequently joined with large fact tables. Replication avoids data shuffling during joins.

  • Random distribution
    Description: Rows are distributed randomly across nodes without a distribution key.
    Recommended scenarios: Tables where there is no clear distribution key or when data is uniform and joins are rare.

  • Hash distribution
    Description: A distribution key is hashed to determine the target node.
    Recommended scenarios: Large fact tables where joins or aggregations are frequently performed on the distribution key, enabling local joins and reducing network traffic.

  • List distribution (available in certain versions)
    Description: Distribution is based on a discrete set of column values.
    Recommended scenarios: Tables that are naturally partitioned by region, category, or other categorical values; can improve partition pruning.

  • Range distribution (available in certain versions)
    Description: Data is distributed according to a numeric range.
    Recommended scenarios: Time-series or ordered data where queries often filter on a range (e.g., date columns).

General guidelines:

  • Use hash distribution on the most frequently joined/grouped column for large fact tables.

  • Use replication for dimension tables that are small (e.g., < 10% of the largest table) and frequently accessed.

  • Use random distribution only when no suitable distribution key exists and joins are infrequent.

  • Use list/range distribution when the table has a natural categorical or temporal segmentation that aligns with query patterns.

All distribution strategies are managed within the gbase database engine, and choosing the right one is critical for achieving linear scalability and high performance in analytical workloads.

Q: openssl sha256sum hash contains output file as part of input when using find command to list the files A:

The redirection is processed by the shell before it runs the find command. Therefore, the file is created before searching starts, and once find runs, it's already there and found. You can

  1. skip the file from find (\! -name hashedoutput.sha256),
  2. filter it out from the output (+ | grep -v '/hashedoutput\.sha256$' > "$1/..."),
  3. create the output elsewhere and move it to the destination later.

Q: How to declare functions in a header file that are defined in a DLL A:

My current problem is that I only have the DLL itself, no headers

If you had stopped right there, then the comments concerning how you will know what these functions actually do and the parameters to pass would more than likely had never occurred.

It is this: SDK or anything like that

that started the ball rolling to a place that you more than likely didn't expect.

If you had documentation, then creating function definitions from what has been documented is straightforward. A four byte integer is int32_t, an ANSI, modifiable character buffer is a char *, an unmodifiable one is const char *, wide character is wchar_t*, etc.

The documentation would have also stated whether the function is stdcall, cdecl or some other calling convention, etc.

__stdcall int FriendlyName1(int arg1, int arg2);

Assuming 1) you have no documentation or 2) you have no sample usage of the DLL's functions, if the DLL is 32-bit, what if arg1 and arg2 are to be treated as pointer values and not just plain integers? Or what if it is an 8-byte integer and not two 4-byte integers?
